Images:
  - [Image #0] The image is a text passage discussing the concept of "Development Hell" in creative projects. The passage is titled "On Development Hell" and explores why some creative works take a long time to complete and often result in disappointment. 
    
    Here is the text from the image:
    
    On Development Hell
    
    Why doesn't development hell work? Creative works or vaporware that survive 'development hell' often disappoint those waiting for them, and often are among the worst things their creators ever make. Duke Nukem Forever, the Star Wars prequel trilogy, Hard To Be A God, Dau, Shenmue III, The Last Dangerous Visions, Rebuild of Evangelion, Juneteenth have not rewarded those who waited years or decades for them as they gradually become punchlines. More broadly, there seems to be relatively little correlation between the amount of time & effort lavished on a work and the resulting quality (the 'equal-odds rule'); as great as a film-maker as Stanley Kubrick was, looking into his working process as recounted by collaborators, it is hard to come away with any conviction that the endless churn of script revision and bizarre random fixations on changes that are reversed the next day yields any net gain rather than delay and expense. Instead of being refined to perfection, they are trapped, or outright degenerate in later revisions.
    
    The resource curse. Why do creative works age like fine milk rather than fine wine? It is not for lack of time, or, often, for resources (especially the pet projects of auteurs). Indeed, ample resources may be something of a curse, allowing a zombie project to linger on long past where any objective third-party would have killed it. (Intellectual property is monopoly, and that means that no one can take away the Star Wars prequels from George Lucas and make a better one, no matter how awful his version may be.)
    
    Development hell is not universal. And it's not intrinsic to creative work period, as we can contrast it with other areas like STEM. Everyone can name examples of development hell blighting fiction or games, but it's much harder to name a scientific or technical or mathematical work which clearly suffered from a 'development hell'; a software program might launch late and be beaten to a punch (Project Xanadu being an exception that prove the rule), and a mathematical proof might be unnecessarily delayed when it would have been adequate published beforehand (there are countless examples of interesting and publishable results in Gauss or Euler or Ramanujan's notebooks, to give 3 famous examples of posthumous publications,

Possible huge problem with psychospiritual journeys: Yes, there are deep structures in the labyrinth of my mind, and yes, I will have profound insights and fundamental shifts when I bring them into full awareness...

And yet...after years of self-work, I'm starting to suspect a large amount of the labyrinth is actually *procedurally generated.* Like a video game map that builds itself on the spot the further you travel across it

It would be like this sequence playing out:
1. I dive deep into the labyrinth of my mind
2. The mind goes "Oh! He's expecting to find some deep structures. Let me generate some of those that are consistent with the rest of me. Oh! He's also expecting to find some enemies there, so let me spawn some demons." 
3. Lo and behold, there is more (eg) "unresolved trauma" to resolve

I think that this process is especially responsive to my motivation. So if I *want* to be in the narrative of Psychospiritual Journey, complete with Shocking Moments Of Insight? (subtext: ...so that I can procrastinate Finding A Job, Building Relationships, Pursuing My Big Scary Calling, etc) ...Well, then the mind will be happy to help. It will procedurally generate an infinite psychospiritual landscape for me to "discover"

I suspect the dynamic I describe above is why many psychospiritual delvers seem like they're just moving in circles. Yes, the mind is vast and there's tons of actually wild stuff in there to explore. Yes, imho Mind is humanity's true final frontier. But also...in some important way...you might be making it up

title: Stop “fixing yourself”—swap the container
summary:
Rich Decibels’ whole thing here is brutally simple: **if you want to change yourself, stop tinkering with “you” and change what you’re *inside of*.** His canonical line—“EVERYTHING THAT LIVES GROWS INSIDE SOMETHING ELSE… so if you want to change yourself, change what you’re inside of”—keeps getting quote-tweeted like it’s a cheat code for escaping atomized self-help brain. In the Oct 2022 thread that kicked this strand into “canon” territory, Rich argues adults already have a huge repertoire; what changes over a life isn’t your internal “stockpile,” it’s your **context, relationships, and environment**. He uses the classic psychedelic/Burning Man “integration” fail as the tell: you don’t integrate by staring harder at your psyche—you integrate by renegotiating your job, friends, and day-to-day container.

Arc-wise it goes: **trigger (Rich crystallizes “insidedness” as anti-self-improvement)** → **peak (community starts applying it everywhere)** → **outcome (it becomes shared vocabulary: containers, sanctums, incubation, canon tweets).** Visakanv makes it practical with “people think their bottleneck is time but it’s actually the absence of a supportive context,” then later goes full systems-midwife: if we took this seriously we’d stop miscarrying relationships/projects/startups. He also nerd-snipes it into *information architecture*: “a good place to put a sanctum is inside another sanctum… a story inside another story… an essay inside another essay,” basically arguing nested containers create sacredness, attention, and freedom to tell truths sideways. Tasshin Fogleman turns it into community scripture (Threadapalooza #25: wombs all the way down) and in 2025 weaponizes it as a compassion post: you’re not broken, you’re under-supported—“have u considered that it ain’t time and it ain’t money and it ain’t ur childhood and it ain’t demons.” Tyler Alterman plugs it into psychospiritual discourse by warning that endless inner-work can be procedurally generated cope; better to **grow new “generator functions”** by surrounding yourself with admired people and beautiful environments (i.e., change the container). Rich’s own sharpened punchline lands in 2024: “you’re going to use your self… to improve your self? the self that needs improving is not a fit tool for making the improvements.”

The residue is a meme/heuristic people actually use: **when you’re stuck, don’t ask “what’s wrong with me?”—ask “what am I inside of?”** It’s sticky because it replaces guilt-y self-optimization with a concrete move: change the room, the schedule, the friends, the job, the structure—build a holding environment where the version of you you want is the default output.
